name: Hyphen test compares chars with == vs compares String objects with ==
side_a: No deduct if the hyphen check compares a primitive char to a char literal (e.g. `username.charAt(i + 1) == '-'`), which is a valid equality test in Java.
side_b: Deduct if the hyphen check compares String objects with `==` (e.g. `username.substring(i + 1, i + 2) == "-"`), since reference comparison instead of `.equals` makes the hyphen detection never reliably fire.

name: Reading one past the current index (charAt(i+1)/substring(i+1,i+2)) without a length guard counts as a real out-of-bounds defect vs. treated as a harmless lookahead idiom
side_a: No_deduct when the lookahead used to detect the hyphen is bounds-safe — either guarded (`i < username.length() - 1 && ...`) or structured so the index can never exceed the last character — and the string actually assembled/returned is correct.
side_b: Deduct when the method peeks at an index that can run past the end of the string (e.g., `username.charAt(i + 1)` evaluated when `i` is the last valid index, or a loop bound of `i <= username.length()`), since the method throws StringIndexOutOfBoundsException instead of returning the shortened name; this is a bounds error, not an excused 'String method called incorrectly'.

name: Comparing String pieces with `==` instead of `.equals` counts as a logic defect that breaks the result vs. a stylistic/API slip excused as 'calling a String method incorrectly'
side_a: No_deduct when the hyphen is detected by a comparison that actually works (char comparison with `==`, or `.equals`/`.compareTo` on substrings), so the hyphen and its neighbor are genuinely skipped.
side_b: Deduct when the hyphen test compares String objects with `==` (e.g., `username.substring(i + 1, i + 2) == "-"`): the condition is never true for the computed substring, so no character is ever skipped and the method returns the unshortened name — an algorithmic failure of the returned value, not an excused malformed method call.
